subject: Compute runway ledger & burst-shaping for Oort Systems dedicated commit
messages:
From: Marissa Cole <marissa@redwood.com>

Subject: Compute runway ledger & burst-shaping for Oort Systems dedicated commit

Hi Aisha / Dave,

Thanks again for the conversation yesterday. Attached is a concise compute runway ledger that maps your expected traffic profile to a recommended Dedicated slab and a burst-shaping policy. High-level summary here so we can iterate quickly:

- Ask: Oort expects GA traffic to peak during weekday business hours with synchronous chat latency SLO of p95 < 350ms for 256-token responses. You also forecast occasional marketing-driven spikes (~3x baseline, 2–3x for short windows).
- Recommendation (initial): 4x H100 GPUs provisioned for baseline SLA coverage, with a 50% burst buffer (2x H100) hot-standby for sustained spikes and failover — operationally 6x H100 allocated.
- Key rationale: we modeled your 45 rps peak (interactive requests) with median generation 80 tokens -> peak tokens/sec ~3,600. Using our rw-13b-int8 profile (mixed prompt distribution) we estimate ~900 tokens/sec per H100 under steady mixed-load conditions. 3,600 / 900 -> 4 GPUs baseline. Add 50% headroom for multi-tenant jitter, KV-cache warmup, and graceful degradation -> 6 GPUs.
- Cost / SLA tradeoffs: this sizing meets p95 < 350ms in our tests for 256-token responses; for tighter latency (p95 < 250ms) we recommend either model downgrade to a faster 7B variant for latency-critical endpoints or a 2x increase in slab count.
- Mitigations: prefix caching (reduces processed tokens by ~18% for repeat prompts), request-level batching windows (50–80ms), and dynamic routing to rw-7b-int8 fallback when 95th percentile latency approaches threshold.

I attached the spreadsheet with the math and a slidedeck of the SLA matrix. Ben / Mina — can you sanity-check the per-GPU throughput numbers and the warmup assumptions by EOD? Once we lock numbers, Kimberly and I will update the commercial commit to reflect the preferred slab/hedge options.

Next steps:
- Internal confirm: throughput per-GPU and warmup assumptions (Ben, Mina)
- Customer decision: preferred hedge policy (2x burst vs. cross-region failover)
- Contract: if Oort signs for a 12-month reserved slab, we can price the 6x H100 configuration with a 10% discount and include two scheduled maintenance blackout windows per quarter.

Thanks —

Marissa Cole
Sr. AE, Strategic Accounts
Redwood Inference

On Tue, Oct 2, 2028 at 09:12 AM Marissa Cole <marissa@redwood.com> wrote:
> Hi Aisha / Dave,
> ...

Aisha — good questions. Quick tech notes and the assumptions baked into the workbook:

- 45 rps mapping: that was the peak ingress observed in your pilot traces (peak observed over a 5m rolling window). For planning we used a conservative business-hours p95 multiplier of 1.4 -> modeled planning peak rps = 63 rps. With median gen length 80 tokens, planned tokens/sec -> 63 * 80 = 5,040 tps. We included both the observed peaks and a 30% event-driven marketing burst allowance in the spreadsheet.

- 900 tokens/sec per H100: this number reflects our measured mixed-workload throughput for rw-13b-int8 with batching enabled (batching window 60ms, dynamic KV cache hit rate ~22%). It is a steady-state number after warmup. Warmup profile: first 10 minutes after a quiet period throughput drops ~35% while KV cache and prefetched KV segments populate; that means ~585 tokens/sec during warmup for a single GPU. We included a 20% additional headroom over warmup to avoid violating p95 SLAs for the first 10m of peak.

- Fallback to rw-7b-int8: our internal measurements show latency improves ~1.8x vs 13B on average for tail latency for short responses (median inference time drops by ~40%). For UX-sensitive endpoints where p95 must be < 250ms we recommend selectively routing to rw-7b-int8 with a quality gate (sanity/eval set) and monitor for semantic drift.

- Quick capacity calc (spreadsheet reference tab: "Capacity_Ledger"):
  * Modeled peak tokens/sec (with p95 multiplier): 5,040 tps
  * Effective per-GPU steady throughput: 900 tps -> baseline GPUs = ceil(5040/900) = 6 GPUs
  * Warmup-adjusted per-GPU: 585 tps -> warmup-safe GPUs = ceil(5040/585) = 9 GPUs
  * Operational compromise: 6 GPUs active + 2 hot spare GPUs with fast onboarding gives effective warmup safety without pre-provisioning 9 GPUs (final operational proposal = 8 GPUs allocated, with autoscale policy to add 1–2 GPUs if sustained >5m over threshold)

Notes: that math diverges a bit from Marissa's initial 4 -> 6 guidance because we applied the p95 multiplier and explicit warmup model. I recommend we present two commercial options to Oort:
  1) Conservative: 8x H100 reserved (recommended for p95 compliance including warmup)
  2) Lean: 6x H100 reserved + 2x burst pool hours billed at premium for short marketing bursts (lower committed ARR)

I'll attach the bench plots and the warmup traces to the workbook.

—Ben
Head of Performance Engineering, Redwood Inference

Aisha / Dave — thanks for the quick read. Short response and proposed decision points for the week:

- We recommend you choose between two commercial configurations:
  A) Conservative (Recommended for SLA-first teams): 8x H100 reserved, includes 2x hot spares for warmup and scheduled pre-warm windows before planned marketing blasts.
  B) Cost-lean: 6x H100 reserved + 2x burst-hour credits/month (auto-provisioned at premium) — lower committed spend, slightly higher operational risk during unplanned sustained spikes.

- Fallback policy: enable dynamic routing to rw-7b-int8 for endpoints tagged "low-fidelity"; keep critical chat endpoints pinned to the 13B family. We will supply a quality gate and an eval harness (Doc: https://docs.redwood.com/notes/oort-compute-playbook) to monitor semantic regressions for 7B fallback.

- Procurement language: Kimberly will own the blackout/maintenance schedule and will add standard SLA carve-outs for scheduled maintenance and model rollout canaries.

Action items:
- Oort: pick A or B by Friday EOD (Oct 6) so we can scope pricing and PO terms.
- Redwood: Ben to attach bench plots & warmup traces; Kimberly to draft contract language; Marissa to update the quote and HubSpot.

Thanks — looking forward to your choice.

Marissa Cole

Redwood Inference
